extracted.intended_audience: medical/laboratory students and histotechnicians learning tissue preparation, staining, and basic microbiology
extracted.subtask_description: Stepwise laboratory procedures and morphological/physiological criteria for preparing, staining, mounting tissue sections (freezing and paraffin methods), plus diagnostic staining techniques and foundational fungal/bacterial classification and morphology for practical lab study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freezing microtome sectioning and mounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the tissue on the plate of a freezing microtome, cover and surround with fresh gum mixture; freeze with ether or preferably carbon dioxide vapour and cut sections; float sections off the knife into tepid water to dissolve gum (about an hour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not required at once, store in 90% alcohol. Transfer with a section lifter to staining fluid; thereafter dehydrate in absolute alcohol, clear in xylol or oil of cloves, and mount in xylol balsam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative rapid freezing method for sections
rubrics_metrics.description: A rapid procedure: cut very small tissue blocks; fix in 10% aqueous formalin for 24 hours; freeze on freezing microtome with CO2 vapour; float sections in tepid water; stain in glass capsules; pick up sections onto a slide submerged obliquely and draw section onto slide; remove folds before final removal from water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After picking up, drain water, drop absolute alcohol to dehydrate, press with folded blotting paper to dry, drop xylol to clear, place a large drop of xylol balsam and lower a cover-glass to mount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraffin method — fixation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix tissue pieces resting on cotton-wool in a wide-mouthed bottle with corrosive sublimate fixing fluid; allow 12–24 hours depending on size. Pour off fixing fluid and wash thoroughly in running water 20–30 minutes to remove excess corrosive sublimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrosive sublimate is the specified fixative here; thorough washing after fixation is required to remove yellow staining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraffin method — hardening/dehydration
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardening: place tissues in successive alcohol strengths (50%, 75%, 90%, absolute) for 12–24 hours each. Dehydration is effected by transferring tissues to fresh absolute alcohol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain times of 12–24 hours in each strength for adequate hardening before clearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraffin method — clearing and infiltration
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearing: place tissue through an alcohol layer floating on chloroform, then transfer to pure chloroform for 6–24 hours until transparent. Infiltration: place cleared tissues in chloroform with pieces of paraffin wax in a warm place about 24 hours; then transfer to pure melted paraffin in a bath at 2°C above the paraffin melting point and soak 4–6 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paraffin with melting-point ≤58°C (54°C recommended). Clearing time varies with tissue size; warmth gradually melts paraffin in infiltration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding, mounting and trimming paraffin blocks
rubrics_metrics.description: Imbed tissue in fresh paraffin in metal/paper moulds: arrange L-shaped mould pieces, pour melted paraffin, place tissue, cool to set in cold water, break off L's and trim excess paraffin retaining rectangular shape; cement block on microtome carrier with melted paraffin; secure by melting paraffin around base if desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When embedding many pieces use stout copper shapes. For storage place blocks in pill-boxes. A hot metal/glass rod can improve adhesion to carrier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cutting paraffin sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut thin sections, and if possible in ribbands, on a paraffin microtome such as Minot, Jung, or Cambridge Rocker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thin, ribboned sections are preferred for ease of mounting and even staining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mounting paraffin sections on slides
rubrics_metrics.description: Float a paraffin section on a large drop of 30% alcohol on the centre of a slide; warm cautiously (Bunsen flame or on paraffin bath) until the section flattens and wrinkles disappear; blot off excess spirit; place slide in a wire rack, section downward, in a hot incubator for 12–24 hours to adhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sections are large/thick or acids are used during staining, add a trace of Mayer's albumin to the alcohol before floating to improve adhesion; 20–30 minutes in incubator suffice when albumin is used. Alternative: paint a thin layer of Schallibaum's solution on slide and heat gently to fix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of Mayer's albumin
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipe: salicylate of soda 1 g, dissolve in glycerine 50 c.c.; add white of egg 50 c.c.; mix thoroughly and filter into a clean bottle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an adhesive additive to alcohol when floating large or difficult sections to ensure firm adhesion during staining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schallibaum's solution for slide adhesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Schallibaum's solution: clove oil 30 c.c., collodion 10 c.c.; keep in a dark blue bottle in a cool place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paint a thin layer on the slide with a camel's hair pencil; lay section on this film and heat gently to fix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staining paraffin sections — general sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Warm the paraffin section to soften, dissolve out wax with xylol, remove xylol by flushing with alcohol. If fixed in corrosive sublimate, treat with Lugol's iodine for two minutes then 90% alcohol to remove yellow staining. Wash in water, stain deeply (single stain), wash, decolourise if necessary, dehydrate in several changes of absolute alcohol, clear in xylol (oil of cloves not usually used as it decolourises), and mount in xylol balsam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stain deeply when using a single stain because subsequent processes decolourise; handle corrosive-subalimate-fixed tissues with iodine treatment to remove yellow tint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-staining: Carmine and Gram-Weigert
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare sections as usual (steps 1–3). Stain in lithium carmine (Orth's) or picrocarmine for 10–30 minutes; wash in picric acid solution until yellow (nuclei red, protoplasm yellow, bacteria colourless); wash in water and alcohol; stain in aniline gentian violet; wash in iodine until dark brown/black; wash, dip in absolute alcohol, decolourise with aniline oil until no more colour discharged; wash with aniline oil/xylol mixture, clear with xylol, mount in xylol balsam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Picric acid solution recipe: saturated picric acid 40 c.c., HCl 1 c.c., 90% alcohol 160 c.c. Steps aim to produce contrasting nuclear/protoplasmic/bacterial colours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative Gram-Weigert method for sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix paraffin section on slide and prepare; stain in alum carmine ~15 minutes; wash; filter aniline gentian violet onto section and stain ~25 minutes; wash; treat with Lugol's iodine until no further darkening; wash; treat with equal parts aniline oil and xylol until no more colour comes away; wash with xylol; decolourise and dehydrate rapidly with absolute alcohol until only faint bluish tint remains; clear with xylol; mount in xylol balsam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fibrin and hyaline tissue stain deep blue; bacteria staining Gram appear deep blue-violet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unna–Pappenheim staining method
rubrics_metrics.description: Stain composition: methylene green 0.15 g, pyronin 0.25 g in carbolic acid 0.5% aqueous solution 78 c.c.; add alcohol 2.5 c.c. and glycerine 20.0 c.c. Method: place tissue in stain for 10 minutes, differentiate and dehydrate in absolute alcohol, clear in xylol, mount in xylol balsam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for differential staining of tissue components; follow differentiation carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating capsules — MacConkey and Friedlaender methods
rubrics_metrics.description: MacConkey: stain as for cover-slip films. Friedlaender's stain: gentian violet (saturated alcoholic) 50 c.c., glacial acetic acid 10 c.c., distilled water 100 c.c.; prepare sections, stain in warm incubator 24 hours, wash, decolourise lightly with 1% acetic acid, dehydrate rapidly with absolute alcohol, clear with xylol, mount in xylol balsam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long warm staining in Friedlaender highlights capsule structure; light decolourisation required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating acid-fast bacilli in sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare sections; stain with haematin 10–20 seconds to get pure nuclear stain and wash; stain with carbolic fuchsin 20–30 minutes at 47°C and wash; treat with 2% aniline hydrochlorate for 2–5 seconds; decolourise in 75% alcohol until section appears free from stain (15–30 minutes); dehydrate in absolute alcohol, clear rapidly with xylol, mount in xylol balsam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carbolic fuchsin at elevated temperature and prolonged decolourisation are crucial to demonstrate acid-fast bacilli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Piridin (Levaditi) method for spirochaetes
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut 1 mm slices; fix in 10% formalin 24 hours; wash 1 hour; place in 96% alcohol 24 hours; transfer to 100 c.c. 1% silver nitrate + 10 g pyridin solution, keep 3 hours at room temp, then 4–6 hours at 50°C; wash in 10% pyridin solution; reduce silver in pyrogallic/acetone/pyridin/distilled water solution for 48 hours; wash, take through alcohols to absolute (20 hours each), clear, embed, cut very thin sections, mount, remove paraffin, clear again and mount in xylol balsam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spirochaetes appear black against pale yellow background. Weak carbol fuchsin, neutral red or toluidin blue may be used to stain background after paraffin removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leishman method for protozoa in sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Reagents: Leishman's Polychrome stain, acetic acid 1/1500, caustic soda 1/7000, distilled water. Mount and remove paraffin, take into distilled water, drain off excess, cover with diluted Leishman (1:2 stain:water) for 5–10 minutes until tissue deep blue, decolourise with acetic acid until only nuclei are blue (examine wet with low power), treat with caustic soda if eosin too marked, wash, rapidly dehydrate with alcohol, clear with xylol, mount in xylol balsam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine during decolourisation with low-power objective to achieve desired contrast; adjust caustic soda to modify eosin tint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical classification of fungi (for lab study)
rubrics_metrics.description: For practical purposes fungi are divided into: 1. Hymenomycetes (mushrooms, etc.), 2. Hyphomycetes (moulds), 3. Blastomycetes (yeasts and torulae), 4. Schizomycetes (bacteria). Note: myxomycetes are now classed as mycetozoa in animal kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a pragmatic, not strictly phylogenetic, classification for laboratory identification and handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphology and reproductive features of Hyphomycetes
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphomycetes composed of a mycelium of jointed rods ('hyphae') from a germinal tube; hyphae are nutritive (submerged) or reproductive (aerial); protoplasm contains granules, pigment, oil globules, sometimes crystals; reproduction: apical spore formation (asexual) and zoospores (sexual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should study non-pathogenic species first to gain technique and because they commonly contaminate preparations. Observe examples (Mucor, Aspergillus, Penicillium, Oidium) and their characteristic structures (sporangium, columella, sterigmata, conidia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphology and reproduction of Blastomycetes
rubrics_metrics.description: Blastomycetes are spherical/oval cells (8–9.5 μ) that multiply by budding and may form a spurious mycelium; contain thin cell-wall, granular protoplasm with vacuoles and sometimes nucleus visible with haematoxylin; reproduce by budding (gemmation) and ascospores (asexual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saccharomyces shows budding and ascospore formation; Torula resembles yeasts but never forms endo-spores—note differences in cell shapes and reproductive behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schizomycetes (bacteria): classification schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacteria may be classified by life function (saprogenic, zymogenic, pathogenic), food requirements (prototrophic, metatrophic, paratrophic), or metabolic products (chromogenic, photogenic, aerogenic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While functional groupings exist, morphological appearances are commonly used for systematic study of fission fungi; no single scientific classification has been universally adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bacterial morphology: shapes and arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Cocci: rounded/oval cells subdivided by post-fission arrangement (diplococci, streptococci, tetrads/merismopedia/pediococci, sarcinae, micrococci/staphylococci). Bacilli: rod-shaped with parallel sides; may form diplobacilli/streptobacilli. Spirilla: curved/twisted filaments classified as spirillum, vibrio (comma), spirochaeta.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrangement after fission is diagnostic; examine stained preparations to determine arrangements and shapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher filamentous bacteria groups and features
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher forms: attached, unbranched, filamentous, show base-apex differentiation, apical growth, exaggerated pleomorphism, pseudo-branching; classified into groups such as Beggiotoa, Thiothrix, Crenothrix, Cladothrix, Leptothrix, Streptothrix (the latter shows true branching and includes pathogenic species).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These forms differ in sulphur granules and branching; use morphology to distinguish groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleomorphism and factors influencing bacterial morphology
rubrics_metrics.description: The morphology of the same bacterium may vary greatly under different conditions — pleomorphism. Factors influencing pleomorphism include composition/reaction of nutrient medium, atmosphere, temperature, and exposure to or protection from light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying morphology, consider culture conditions as they can dramatically affect observed forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bacterial anatomical structures to observe
rubrics_metrics.description: Key anatomical features: capsule (gelatinous envelope, may cement cells into zoogloea), cell wall (protective outer layer, may show plasmolysis), cell contents (protoplasm, vacuoles, oil globules, chromatin granules, sulphur granules), polar granules/metachromatic bodies, and flagella (organs of locomotion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some species show prominent capsules (e.g., B. pneumoniae); plasmolysis and polar granules aid identification; flagella are not pseudopodia and their arrangement is taxonomically informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of flagellation (ciliation) and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Flagella types: polar — monotrichous (single at one pole), amphitrichous (single at each pole), lophotrichous (tuft at pole); diffuse — peritrichous (flagella scattered around periphery). Examples: monotrichous B. pyocyaneus; amphitrichous Spirillum volutans; lophotrichous B. cyanogenus; peritrichous B. typhosus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flagellar arrangement helps in distinguishing species; examine appropriate preparations to visualize flagella.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bacterial reproduction — active (fission) stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Vegetative reproduction by fission: cell elongates, protoplasm aggregates at poles, a circular constriction forms mid-cell and a septum develops, division deepens forming two cells which may remain united for a variable time before separating and further dividing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe fission stages in hanging-drop cultures or stained preparations to appreciate division morphology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resting stage — spore formation types and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Spore formation: arthrogenous (in micrococci, relative increase of resistance, not true spores) and endogenous (spore formed within cell protoplasm with distinct spore membrane — exosporium and endosporium). Spore characteristics: difficult to stain/decolourise, highly refractile, highly resistant to heat/desiccation/starvation, resistance varies by species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all bacteria form spores; spore formation influenced by nutrient exhaustion, toxic metabolites, and unfavorable environment. Most spores are killed by prolonged boiling (ten minutes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of spore-bearing bacilli (morphological forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification by parent cell shape during sporulation: (A) parent unaltered; (B) parent altered — Clostridium (rod swollen at centre, attenuated poles, spindle-shaped), Cuneate (wedge-shaped), Clavate (swollen at one pole, keyhole-shaped), Capitate (spherical enlargement at one pole, drumstick-shaped).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape alterations during sporulation serve as a basis for classification of spore-bearing bacilli; note examples like B. tetani (capitate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Germination of spores — stages and modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Germination: spores swell by water absorption, lose refrangibility, then follow one of three species-constant processes: (a) grow out into bacillus without discarding spore membrane; (b) lose spore membrane by solution; (c) lose spore membrane by rupture (polar, bipolar, or equatorial). New vegetative bacillus forms and undergoes fission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe germination in hanging-drop cultures; the mode of membrane loss and timing are species-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nutritional requirements and food-stuff categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Organic foods: pure parasites (e.g., B. leprae) cannot live outside the body; facultative parasites require highly organized foods (proteids) and salts; saprophytic bacteria are more easily cultivated (some grow in distilled water or pure carbohydrate solutions). Water is essential for growth. Growth is most active in media slightly acid to phenolphthalein (neutral or faintly alkaline to litmus), whereas moulds favor strongly acid media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose culture media and conditions based on organism type; ensure water availability and appropriate pH reaction for bacteria versus moulds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental factors affecting bacterial growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Atmosphere: obligate aerobes need oxygen; facultative anaerobes tolerate both; obligate anaerobes require absence of oxygen. Temperature: little growth below 5°C or above 40°C; 30–37°C optimal for many; bacteria classified by optimum temperature (psychrophilic, mesophilic, thermophilic) with typical min/opt/max ranges. Light: may impede growth or alter biochemical properties; pathogenic bacteria often lose virulence under light. Movements/agitation: violent shaking kills bacteria; rest favors growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider oxygen availability, incubation temperature ranges, and light exposure when culturing; note thermal death-point (temperature killing vegetative forms in 10 minutes) as a biological constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metabolic products: pigments, light and enzymes
rubrics_metrics.description: Pigment production: chromogenic bacteria classified by pigment destination — chromoparous (pigment diffused into medium), chromophorous (pigment stored in protoplasm), parachromophorous (pigment in cell wall). Light production: some water-derived bacteria are photogenic and show phosphorescence under suitable conditions. Enzyme production: many bacteria produce soluble ferments/enzymes evidenced by liquefaction of gelatine, clotting of milk, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe pigment, bioluminescence and enzymatic effects as diagnostic metabolic traits; production can depend on environmental conditions (oxygen, light, temperature).
